title: What changed in practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, what surprised you, and your line: surprised. Musa, a boat, a wall, and a year that went somewhere unexpected. Did you write your surprise down, or tell someone? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

Good, or silent. Tie it, trust Him. Count before you are counted. The right hand, the name. Plant it anyway. Start next door. All year the lessons have ended with a short line and one small thing to try. A line like that can be said once and drift off with the day. That is how lines work. But maybe one didn't. Maybe a bismillah before meals is still there. Maybe a pause before speaking, or a coin set aside each week, or a quick check of the heart before sleep. Today, the habit that stuck.
screen: `GOOD, OR SILENT. TIE IT, TRUST HIM.` → `A LINE CAN DRIFT OFF.` → `ONE MAY HAVE STUCK.`

segments.voice: First, a hadith the year met at the charity jar. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha reports, in paraphrase, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was asked which deeds are most beloved to Allah, and he said: the most constant of them, even if they are small. Not the biggest. Not the most dramatic. The ones that keep going. Second, how he lived it. Asked whether he set aside special days for extra worship, Aisha answered, in paraphrase, that his deeds were constant, like steady rain, and that none of them could do what he did. Third, why small and constant. The year kept circling back to it. The boy at the platter got three short instructions and kept them for life. The Muwatta's line on character, the hadith on the heart, the tied camel: all of them are practices for an ordinary Tuesday, not a once-a-year push. The habits the year asked for were small enough to survive a bad day. Fourth, if nothing stuck. The hadith does not ask for a list. It asks for one thing, kept. And the Qur'an tells those who have wronged themselves, in paraphrase, not to despair of Allah's mercy. Muslims call coming back tawbah, one of the stations the year studied: turning, and beginning again. So whatever stuck, or didn't, the question for tomorrow is the same. What is one small thing, and will it still be there when the day is hard?
screen: `THE MOST CONSTANT, EVEN IF SMALL.` · `HIS DEEDS WERE LIKE STEADY RAIN.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO SURVIVE A BAD DAY.` · `IF NOTHING STUCK, BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep it tomorrow. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Look back over the year for one habit that is still with you, however small. If you find one, notice it, and be glad of it. If you don't, choose one now from the year's lines, small enough to keep. Then picture tomorrow: the exact moment it will happen. The kettle, the doorway, the first bite, the last light. See yourself doing it there. Hold that picture for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
What changed in practice. The one habit from the year that kept going, small and constant, the kind the hadith calls most beloved. Today's word.
Your line: it stuck. Today, do your one habit once more, on purpose, and tomorrow do it again at the moment you pictured. Tomorrow, what you still ask. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers encourage small, regular acts over occasional big ones, such as a fixed daily portion of Qur'an, a set extra prayer, or a regular charity, citing the hadith that the most beloved deeds are the most constant, even if small.

fork.setup: a friend says that from tomorrow she'll read the Qur'an for an hour every night, though she hasn't opened it in months. what fits today's hadith?
options: an hour or nothing; small amounts don't count.
start with a few verses a night that she can keep, even on a hard day.
wait for Ramadan and do it all then.
fork.reveal: the most beloved deeds are the most constant, even if small: a few verses kept beat an hour dropped.

original.note: Arabic: the most constant of them, the hadith's word for the deeds most beloved to Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: real change means a big transformation.
what it means: in the hadith, the deeds most beloved to Allah are the constant ones, even if small.
what a scholar hears: adwamuha wa in qall, the most constant even if little, and Aisha's description of his deeds as dimah, steady rain.

notes: Confirm numbering of Bukhari 6464 and 6466 and that 'like steady rain' fairly renders dimah in Aisha's description; 'none of you could do what he did' paraphrases the same report.
Original أدومها and the transliteration 'adwamuha wa in qall': confirm vocalization.
The teach head 'small enough to survive a bad day' is the script's own framing, not a cited claim.
